No whiteboards. No trick questions. Just real-world engineering. Here is a breakdown of all 7 rounds.
If you have spent any time interviewing in Big Tech, you are probably exhausted by the standard loop. You spend weeks grinding LeetCode, memorizing dynamic programming algorithms you will never use in production, and practicing how to reverse a binary tree on a whiteboard.
Recently, I interviewed for a Senior Software Engineer role at Stripe.
Going into it, I had heard rumors that their interview process was different. After going through all 7 rounds (including the online assessment), I can confirm the rumors are true. Stripe’s interview loop is the most pragmatic, realistic, and forward-thinking process I have experienced in my career.
They don’t test your ability to memorize algorithms. They test your ability to do the actual job and in 2026, that includes how you manage AI.
Here is exactly what happened in each round, and what they are actually evaluating you on.
Round 1: The Online Assessment (OA)
The process kicked off with a HackerRank assessment. But instead of a generic algorithmic puzzle, it was a multi-part problem statement that mirrored real-world logic.
The setup: You are given a base problem. Once you write code to get all the initial test cases passing, the next part of the problem unlocks, adding new requirements or constraints to your existing codebase.
What they are evaluating: They are testing your ability to write extensible code. If you hardcode a messy solution for Part 1, you will completely block yourself from solving Part 2. You have to write clean, modular code from the very first keystroke.
Round 2: The Pairing Round
This was effectively a live version of the OA. You are paired with an engineer and asked to solve an iterative problem.
What they are evaluating: It is not just about getting to the right answer; it is about how you get there.

• Communication: Can you articulate your thought process clearly before you start typing?

• Structure: Are you applying SOLID principles on the fly?

• Speed: You need to translate your thoughts into working code quickly.
Round 3: The Bug Bash
This was by far my favorite round, because it is exactly what you do during your first week at a new job.
The interviewer gives you a URL to clone a repository in your language of choice. The codebase has a specific bug in it, and your task is to track it down and fix it.
What they are evaluating: Here is the secret to the Bug Bash they don’t actually care if you fix the bug. They are evaluating your navigation and debugging philosophy. When dropped into a completely foreign codebase, what is your first move? Do you blindly start console.loging everywhere? Or do you run the test suite, read the stack trace, use a debugger, and trace the data flow logically? They want to see how you investigate the unknown.
Round 4: API Integration
In this round, the interviewer hands you an API endpoint and a link to its documentation. Your task is to write a script that authenticates, calls the API, parses the response, and performs some business logic with the data.
What they are evaluating: Real-world tool proficiency. You need to be deeply familiar with at least one networking or HTTP library in your language (e.g., requests in Python, or axios/fetch in Node.js). They are watching how quickly you can read documentation, understand a JSON payload, and handle network errors or edge cases.
Round 5: AI-Assisted Coding
This round proves how modern Stripe’s hiring has become. They gave me a problem statement similar to the OA, but the catch was that I had to use an AI agent to write the code.
What they are evaluating: They want to see if you treat AI like an omniscient wizard or like a junior developer. If you blindly copy-paste the prompt into the AI and accept whatever spaghetti code it spits out, you will fail. They are looking for Senior engineers who understand the requirements deeply, break the problem down into architecture, and then instruct the AI with specific constraints (e.g., “Implement this using a factory pattern, ensure the variables are strictly typed, and handle these three edge cases”). It tests your ability to do code review and prompt architecture in real-time.
Round 6: System Design
I was asked to design a core financial system.
Unlike generic system design interviews where you can just throw Kafka and a NoSQL database at the problem to achieve massive scale, designing for a payment processor requires a different mindset.
What they are evaluating: Consistency. In the financial domain, a dropped message or a duplicated transaction isn’t just a bug; it is a catastrophe. They are looking for holistic thinking. You need to talk deeply about idempotency keys, two-phase commits, relational database ACID guarantees, and how you design a system where the data is perfectly consistent across distributed nodes.
Round 7: The Manager Sync
The final round was a behavioral and experience dive with the Hiring Manager.
What they are evaluating: Alignment. We discussed my past projects, my approach to engineering leadership, and how I handle team conflicts and project prioritization. They want to ensure your working style matches the high-agency, writing-heavy culture of the team you are joining.
3 Takeaways to Pass the Stripe Interview
If you have a Stripe loop coming up, throw away the LeetCode hard problems and focus on these three things:

• Master One Language Thoroughly: You cannot rely on auto-complete or Google for basic syntax during the API or Bug Bash rounds. Know your standard library, your HTTP clients, and your testing frameworks cold.

• Prioritize Speed & Execution: The practical rounds move fast. You need to be comfortable typing quickly, setting up a local environment instantly, and iterating without hesitation.

• Breathe SOLID Principles: Because the coding rounds are iterative, your code structure matters as much as the output. If you don’t use Object-Oriented Programming principles effectively, your codebase will collapse under the weight of the new requirements.
Stripe’s interview process demands that you be a competent, hands-on software engineer who knows how to leverage modern tools. It is rigorous, but it is deeply fair.
Over to you: What are your thoughts on companies introducing an “AI-Assisted Coding” round into the interview loop? Is this the future of tech hiring? Let me know in the comments.
